title: How RL Reshapes LLM Reasoning: Transferability, Coverage, and Scaling Laws

paper.title: How RL Reshapes LLM Reasoning: Transferability, Coverage, and Scaling Laws
paper.abstract:
Abstract Recent studies on reinforcement learning (RL) report seemingly conflicting evidence about large language model (LLM) reasoning. Training on mathematics can improve performance in other domains, yet gains in Pass@1 can coincide with lower Pass@ N \displaystyle N than the base model. This raises a fundamental question: does RL expand an LLM’s reasoning boundary, or merely reweight its existing reasoning space? We revisit these phenomena across Qwen and Gemma model families, showing both cross-domain gains and forgetting, while coverage at large sampling budgets increases on some tasks and decreases on others.
Detailed analysis of solution traces before and after RL indicates a shift in the reasoning strategies the model employs, motivating a two-stage autoregressive policy model that separates strategy selection from problem-specific execution.
Within this framework, we prove how RL’s implicit bias reshapes strategy preferences, allowing gains on some tasks while suppressing strategies required by others. This mechanism can also broaden or narrow coverage at a given sampling budget even without expanding strategy support.
We further provide theoretical justifications for log-sigmoid and log-linear scaling laws in RL compute, and evaluate their predictive power.
Together, these results connect changes in strategy selection to cross-domain transfer, reasoning coverage, and compute scaling.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement learning (RL) has improved the performance of large language models (LLMs) on reasoning tasks ( shao2024deepseekmath ; deepseekai2025r1 ; yu2025dapo ) . RL updates a model using reward feedback on sampled responses, rather than training it to imitate demonstrations. Its success on mathematics and coding raises a broader question about how RL reshapes LLM reasoning. What accounts for these gains remains debated. RL may teach a model new ways to reason, or make it more likely to use reasoning it can already produce. For example, RL training on mathematical problems can improve performance in other domains ( huan2025transferability ) , but such gains are compatible with either interpretation. Sampling provides another perspective. Gains in one-shot accuracy (Pass@1) can accompany lower Pass@ N \displaystyle N , the fraction of problems solved within N \displaystyle N sampled attempts ( yue2504does ) , while prolonged training has been reported to broaden coverage ( liu2025prorl ) . These findings motivate the central question. Does RL expand an LLM’s reasoning boundary, or merely reweight its existing reasoning space? Our experiments show that training can improve performance in its own domain while reducing performance on other tasks or lowering Pass@1024 ( Figures 1 and 2 ). Comparing Qwen trajectories before and after RL indicates a shift in the model’s preferences among reasoning strategies ( Section 3.1 ). This motivates a two-stage policy model that separates strategy selection from problem-specific execution. Within this framework, we characterize how the implicit bias of RL reshapes strategy preferences, improving performance on some tasks while suppressing strategies required by others. We also contrast this mechanism with supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Our focus on how strategy preferences generalize across tasks complements the analyses of training-prompt sharpening and coverage ( chen2026reshaping ; chen2025coverage ) . Crucially, this reweighting mechanism explains coverage shifts without introducing new strategies. Pass@ N \displaystyle N at large N \displaystyle N is especially sensitive to problems with low success probabilities. Amplifying or suppressing rare valid strategies can broaden or narrow benchmark coverage, even as Pass@1 improves. Recent studies also examine how performance scales with RL compute ( khatri2025scalerl ; meta2026musespark ) . Our framework connects strategy selection to scaling laws, showing that selection dynamics admit log-sigmoid and log-linear approximations. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We document task-specific RL transfer and forgetting alongside divergent coverage shifts, with outcomes dictated by the training data, evaluation benchmark, and base model ( Section 2 ). • We analyze Qwen solution trajectories and find changes in which strategies are sampled for a question, motivating a separation of strategy selection from execution ( Sections 3.1 and 3.2 ). • Theoretically, we characterize RL’s implicit bias in strategy selection and derive conditions for transfer, forgetting, and expansion or shrinkage of coverage at a given sampling budget ( Sections 4 and 5 ). • We derive local approximation bounds for log-sigmoid and log-linear scaling laws and evaluate how well the fitted curves predict performance later in training, showing that predictive reliability varies with the training mixture and evaluation domain ( Section 6 ).

sections.heading: 2 Empirical Evidence on Transfer and Reasoning Coverage
sections.text: The extent to which RL transfers beyond its training domain and expands the reasoning boundary remains actively debated. In this section, we revisit these phenomena across various model families and task domains to show that these seemingly contradictory findings can be reconciled.

sections.heading: Models and datasets.
sections.text: Our experiments use Qwen3-14B-Base ( yang2025qwen3 ) and Gemma-3-12B-IT ( gemmateam2025gemma3 ) as base models. We train both models on 48K mathematics problems from UniReason ( huan2025transferability ) (Math RL). For Qwen, we also train a variant on this dataset augmented with 5K curated coding problems from Eurus-2-RL ( cui2025process ) (Math-Code RL). For comparison, we also train both models with SFT using 40K mathematics demonstrations obtained by rejection sampling on Qwen3-32B responses ( huan2025transferability ) .

sections.heading: Training setup.
sections.text: For all RL experiments, we train with GRPO ( shao2024deepseekmath ) using verl ( sheng2024hybridflow ) for 200 steps at a learning rate of 10 − 6 \displaystyle 10^{-6} . Each step samples 512 prompts and generates 16 responses per prompt (up to 16,384 tokens), followed by one epoch of actor updates with a minibatch size of 128. For SFT, we train for 1.5 epochs using a batch size of 512 and a learning rate of 5 × 10 − 5 \displaystyle 5\times 10^{-5} . Further training details are given in Appendix D .

sections.heading: Evaluation protocol.
sections.text: We evaluate transfer using benchmarks of mathematics, coding, knowledge and planning, and general capabilities. Our default inference settings use temperature 0.6, top- p \displaystyle p 0.95, and a maximum generation length of 32,768 tokens, though specific benchmarks retain their original protocols such as greedy decoding. Section D.2 gives the benchmark list and complete task-specific sampling and scoring details.

sections.heading: 2.2 Cross-domain transfer and forgetting
sections.text: Figure 1 : Transfer and forgetting depend on the benchmark, training data, and base model. Each column reports changes in performance from the base model after training. RL consistently improves in-domain performance, but transfer behavior beyond the mathematics and coding domains varies significantly. In contrast, SFT exhibits catastrophic forgetting across a broad range of domains. Figure 1 illustrates the transfer and forgetting results. While RL consistently improves in-domain math performance, out-of-domain (OOD) behavior diverges significantly. Incorporating coding data into training (Qwen3-Math-Code-RL) improves coding tasks but fails to yield universal transfer. Moreover, despite identical training data, Qwen3-Math-RL and Gemma-3-Math-RL shift in opposite directions on many OOD tasks. SFT results exhibit similar model dependence: Qwen3-SFT shows selective transfer on knowledge and planning despite broad forgetting elsewhere, whereas Gemma-3-SFT suffers universal OOD degradation. Together, these results indicate that training-domain success does not reliably predict OOD outcomes. Instead, transferability emerges from the complex interaction among training data, evaluation benchmark, and base model . Complete scores are reported in Table 1 . Although prior work suggests that RL can generalize better to OOD tasks than SFT ( huan2025transferability ; chu2025sft ) , our findings highlight that RL remains susceptible to forgetting, with the direction and magnitude of OOD performance changes varying substantially across settings ( chen2026retaining ; shenfeld2026razor ) .

sections.heading: 2.3 Expansion and shrinkage of finite-budget coverage
sections.text: Figure 2 : RL can either expand or contract reasoning coverage at large sampling budgets. Higher Pass@1 can accompany either lower or higher Pass@1024 relative to the base model. The direction of the coverage change varies across training mixtures, benchmarks, and base models. Task-level gains and losses show how training changes performance across domains. To examine how it changes the range of problems solved within each task, we compare coverage at different sampling budgets using Pass@ N \displaystyle N ( Figure 2 ). For a fixed prompt, Pass@ N \displaystyle N increases with Pass@1; however, benchmark-level comparisons do not necessarily preserve the Pass@1 ordering at large N \displaystyle N .

sections.heading: Reduced coverage at large sampling budgets.
sections.text: The most prevalent pattern we observe is higher Pass@1 alongside lower Pass@1024 relative to the base model, especially in mathematics. This agrees with the coverage contrast reported by yue2504does .

sections.heading: Broader coverage when base success is rare.
sections.text: On the Reasoning Gym task BoxNet ( stojanovski2026reasoning ) , where the base model’s success is exceptionally rare, Qwen3-Math-RL raises Pass@1 from 3.8% to 9.9% and Pass@1024 from 34.0% to 51.0%. Gemma-3-Math-RL also raises Pass@1024 coverage, although its Pass@1 falls. Qwen’s joint gains show that higher one-shot accuracy can accompany higher Pass@1024, consistent with liu2025prorl ; wen2026reinforcement . Our observations are broadly consistent with prior work ( liu2025prorl ) : shifts in Pass@ N \displaystyle N are largely dictated by the benchmark distribution and the base model’s initial ability, with substantial gains generally emerging where initial coverage is low. We further find that the training data itself can alter this regime: Qwen3-Math-RL and Qwen3-Math-Code-RL move CodeContests coverage in opposite directions. Consequently, whether RL expands or shrinks finite-budget coverage is context-dependent, rather than a universal RL effect or a trend that can be inferred from Pass@1. We examine the solution trajectories underlying these contrasts in Section 3.1 .

sections.heading: 3 From Empirical Observations to Reasoning Strategy Selection
sections.text: To understand the performance and coverage changes in Sections 2.2 and 2.3 , we compare solution trajectories before and after RL. The comparison indicates a shift in the strategies used to solve a question. We describe these strategies as reasoning routes and examine how their use differs between the base and RL models. The findings motivate a model that separates strategy selection from conditional answer generation ( Section 3.2 ).

sections.heading: 3.1.1 Analysis setup
sections.text: We compare Qwen3-14B-Base with Qwen3-Math-RL on 240 questions from six benchmarks, with 16 responses per model and question. A reasoning route is the strategy used to reach a response’s final conclusion, when identifiable. Route identity reflects the problem representation and key mechanism, not notation, arithmetic, or final answers. For example, analytic reduction and exhaustive search are different routes. For each question, we combine both models’ strategy descriptions extracted by an LLM from their reasoning traces and group them by route. We average the number of distinct routes over equally sized samples of identifiable responses from both models, using the smaller number of identifiable responses available for each question, and then average equally over questions. Separately, we check which RL routes appear among the question’s original 16 base responses. Appendix E gives classification and statistical details.

sections.heading: 3.1.2 Empirical findings
sections.text: Figure 3 : RL uses fewer routes, but also routes absent from base samples. (a) Mean numbers of distinct routes, using equal numbers of identifiable responses from both models for each question. (b) Percentage of RL responses whose route is absent from the same question’s 16 base responses.

sections.heading: RL concentrates on fewer routes per question.
sections.text: Figure 3 (a) shows lower mean route counts for Qwen3-Math-RL on all six benchmarks, with the largest decreases on coding benchmarks. Across questions, the mean falls from 3.24 for the base model to 2.66 for RL, with a paired difference (RL minus base) of − 0.58 \displaystyle-0.58 (95% confidence interval [ − 0.78 , − 0.38 ] \displaystyle[-0.78,-0.38] ). For example, a LiveCodeBench question asks for the minimum absolute difference between array elements at least x \displaystyle x indices apart. Its 16 base responses use three routes, including comparison of neighboring values found by binary search, which all 16 RL responses use.

sections.heading: RL also uses routes absent from the base samples.
sections.text: Of 3,840 Qwen3-Math-RL responses, 487 (12.7%) follow a route absent from the base responses to the same question ( Figure 3 (b)). For example, on a LiveCodeBench question finding pattern occurrences within distance k \displaystyle k of another pattern’s occurrence, all 16 base responses compare occurrence pairs directly, whereas 11 RL responses use binary search over occurrence lists.

sections.text: Beyond transfer and reasoning coverage, recent studies ask how performance scales with RL compute. khatri2025scalerl introduce a log-sigmoid law: R ⁡ ( C ) = R 0 + A − R 0 1 + ( C mid / C ) B . R(C)=R_{0}+\frac{A-R_{0}}{1+(C_{\rm mid}/C)^{B}}. Alternatively, several works ( meta2026musespark ; tan2026scaling ; shen2026understanding ) apply a first-order approximation to derive a log-linear law: R ⁡ ( C ) = R 0 + B lin ​ log ⁡ ( C / C ref ) . sections.heading: 6.1 Empirical scaling laws in RL
sections.text: Figure 4 : Scaling behavior of RL compute. Both laws capture the fitting regime effectively with 𝖱 𝟤 > 0.99 \displaystyle\mathsf{R^{2}}>0.99 on average. Extrapolative predictions are highly reliable up to 2 × \displaystyle\times compute in the math domain and average scores, yet exhibit greater variation on coding and planning tasks due to noisy RL training dynamics. We fit Eqs. 6.1 and 6.2 to Qwen3-Math-RL and Qwen3-Math-Code-RL evaluations through step 200, using cumulative GPU-hours as compute. We extend both RL runs to step 350 to test predictions beyond the range of compute used for fitting, where the cumulative compute is nearly 2 × \displaystyle 2\times the fitting budget. Figure 4 shows the observed scores and fitted curves during fitting and extrapolation. Detailed fitting procedures, coefficient estimates, and results using other compute metrics are given in Section D.4 . As shown in Figure 4 , the log-sigmoid and log-linear fits are often nearly indistinguishable over the range of compute used for fitting. This is expected because the log-linear law in eq. 6.2 locally approximates the log-sigmoid law in eq. 6.1 . The laws diverge only during extrapolation: the log-linear law maintains a constant rate of improvement with log compute and is therefore unbounded, whereas the log-sigmoid law bends toward a finite plateau. During the additional training, Qwen3-Math-RL follows the log-linear prediction more closely, yet Qwen3-Math-Code-RL exhibits saturation: the log-sigmoid curve better tracks late-stage performance on MATH500, AIME, and ACPBench, as well as the average scores. Meanwhile, the log-linear model increasingly overpredicts performance at higher compute budgets. The reliability of scaling-law predictions also varies by evaluation domain. In-domain mathematical benchmarks consistently follow the fitted predictions, whereas extrapolation to coding and planning benchmarks is more brittle. Individual benchmark trajectories are also less stable than their average, reflecting the noisy dynamics of practical RL training. Notably, while khatri2025scalerl ; tan2026scaling also report extrapolative scaling laws, their evaluations are restricted to held-out data drawn from the training distribution. In contrast, our analysis incorporates out-of-distribution and cross-domain evaluations. Our setting therefore tests not only whether performance scales predictably with RL compute, but also whether this scaling behavior transfers to new domains.

sections.heading: Reinforcement learning for LLM reasoning and chain of thought.
sections.text: CoT prompting and self-consistency establish the value of generating and sampling reasoning trajectories ( wei2022chain ; wang2023selfconsistency ) . Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains models using automatically checked task outcomes; Tülu 3 incorporates this approach into an open post-training recipe ( lambert2024tulu ) . shao2024deepseekmath introduces GRPO, and DeepSeek-R1 demonstrates large-scale reasoning gains from RL ( deepseekai2025r1 ) . DAPO and Open-Reasoner-Zero further develop open systems for scaling RL training on reasoning tasks ( yu2025dapo ; hu2025openreasonerzero ) . liu2025understanding examine how base-model capabilities and biases in GRPO affect training, and introduce Dr. GRPO to improve token efficiency.

sections.heading: Transferability, forgetting, and the reasoning boundary.
sections.text: chu2025sft find that RL trained with outcome rewards generalizes better than SFT to unseen textual rules and visual variants in arithmetic and navigation tasks. huan2025transferability find that RL transfers more broadly and retains performance better than SFT in controlled experiments, while cheng2025crossdomain show that transfer varies with training domain and task difficulty. chen2026retaining identify on-policy data as a major factor in RL’s relative resistance to forgetting. Coverage findings also differ: yue2504does observe gains at small sampling budgets but reduced coverage at large ones, whereas liu2025prorl report expansion under prolonged RL training. wen2026reinforcement further show that evaluating reasoning correctness, rather than final answers alone, can change coverage comparisons. Our framework characterizes conditions for these contrasting outcomes within a shared model of strategy selection, distinguishing coverage at a given sampling budget from the creation or loss of underlying strategies.

sections.heading: Scaling laws in reinforcement learning.
sections.text: khatri2025scalerl fit log-sigmoid curves relating compute to performance and validate extrapolation to longer RL runs. Meta’s Muse Spark reports log-linear gains in training scores with increasing RL steps ( meta2026musespark ) . tan2026scaling study joint scaling with model size, data, and compute in mathematical reasoning, while shen2026understanding relate the returns from increasing RL compute to pretraining. These studies establish empirical scaling relationships, but do not derive the commonly used log-sigmoid and log-linear forms from RL training dynamics. Our work provides a theoretical justification for both forms by deriving them as approximations to the dynamics of reasoning strategy selection, with explicit error bounds. We also examine their predictive reliability across evaluation domains.

sections.heading: Theoretical analyses of RL in LLMs.
sections.text: chen2026reshaping analyze the selection of reasoning patterns in a two-stage tabular policy with fixed conditional success rates, focusing on behavior on training prompts. Complementary analyses study how gradient gaps affect optimization stability ( suk2025optimization ) , success amplification under GRPO ( mroueh2025grpo ) , and pretrained response coverage ( chen2025coverage ) . Our framework learns both strategy and answer policies and uses shared prompt features to derive how source updates reweight target strategies. This mechanism connects strategy selection to transfer and forgetting, Pass@ N \displaystyle N coverage, and scaling laws that describe performance over a limited range of training compute.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion and Discussion
sections.text: In this paper, we investigate how RL reshapes LLM reasoning. Starting from empirical observations across model families and task domains, we analyze solution traces before and after RL, showing a shift in the distribution over reasoning strategies. We propose a two-stage policy model to formalize this phenomenon and prove the conditions under which RL can transfer or forget capabilities and expand or contract finite-budget coverage. We also use this model to give a theoretical justification for empirical scaling laws in RL compute. These results connect changes in strategy selection to cross-domain transfer, reasoning coverage, and compute scaling.

sections.heading: RL.
sections.text: We run GRPO in verl with a learning rate of 10 − 6 \displaystyle 10^{-6} for 200 steps. Each step samples 512 prompts and 16 responses per prompt, followed by one PPO epoch with a minibatch size of 128 prompts. Training rollouts use temperature 1, top- p \displaystyle p 1, a 2,048-token prompt limit, and a 16,384-token response limit. The lower and upper clipping parameters are 0.2 and 0.28. Mathematics rewards indicate final-answer correctness, while coding rewards measure the fraction of ten tests passed.

sections.heading: SFT.
sections.text: We use batch size 512, learning rate of 5 × 10 − 5 \displaystyle 5\times 10^{-5} , a two-epoch cosine schedule with 10% warmup, and a 16,384-token sequence limit. We evaluate the model after 1.5 epochs of training (step 117).

sections.heading: Benchmarks.
sections.text: We evaluate transfer and forgetting across four domains: 1. Math : MATH500 [ hendrycks2021math ] , AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and OMEGA [ sun2025omega ] ; 2. Coding : LiveCodeBench [ jain2024livecodebench ] , CodeContests [ li2022alphacode ] , and DELTA [ sun2025rlgrok ] ; 3. Knowledge and Planning : GPQA-Diamond [ rein2023gpqa ] , HEAD-QA [ vilares2019headqa ] , ACPBench [ kokel2025acpbench ] , ToolUse [ tang2023toolalpaca ] , and Science [ feng2024sciknoweval ] ; 4. General Capabilities : CoQA [ reddy2019coqa ] , IFEval [ zhou2023ifeval ] , HaluEval [ li2023halueval ] , MC-TACO [ zhou2019mctaco ] , WildJailbreak [ jiang2024wildteaming ] , and WildGuardTest [ han2024wildguard ] .

sections.heading: Evaluation protocol.
sections.text: We use native chat templates. Sampled reasoning tasks use temperature 0.6, top- p \displaystyle p 0.95, top- k \displaystyle k 20, and a maximum generation length of 32,768 tokens. We sample three responses per problem for MATH500 and GPQA-Diamond, 10 for LiveCodeBench, 32 for AIME, and one for DELTA. CodeContests uses Eurus-2-RL’s 377-problem validation subset. For greedy decoding, the maximum response length is 32,768 tokens for ACPBench, CoQA, and HaluEval, and 4,096 tokens for ToolUse, Science, and the safety benchmarks. HEAD-QA and MC-TACO use likelihood scoring; IFEval uses one response. We retain native task metrics, including strict instruction-level IFEval accuracy, CoQA F1, DELTA test pass rates, and WildGuard-based refusal accuracy.

sections.heading: Appendix E Reasoning-Route Analysis
sections.text: This appendix provides implementation details, examples, and prompt templates for the reasoning-route analysis in Section 3.1 .

sections.heading: Questions and generation setup.
sections.text: The analysis in Section 3.1 compares Qwen3-14B-Base with Qwen3-Math-RL at step 200 using 16 responses per model for each of 240 questions from MATH500, AIME 2024, AIME 2025, GPQA-Diamond, CodeContests, and LiveCodeBench. Responses use temperature 0.7, top- p \displaystyle p 0.95, no top- k \displaystyle k truncation ( top- ​ k = − 1 \displaystyle\text{top-}k=-1 ), and a maximum generation length of 16,384 tokens. The 16 responses per model and question use sampling seeds 0 through 15.

sections.heading: Route definition.
sections.text: Following Section 3.1 , a reasoning route is the strategy a response uses to reach its conclusion. A route is identifiable when the response contains enough reasoning or code about the question to identify a solution method. The method need not be correct or complete: a program with errors or an unfinished solution can reveal a route, whereas a final answer alone does not. Each identifiable response receives one label for its primary route: the method used to reach its final conclusion or produce its submitted program. If this is unclear, we choose the most developed method, breaking ties by choosing the first method supported by reasoning or code. Routes differ in how they represent the problem or in their main idea, not in notation, mistakes within the same method, or whether it is carried out by hand or in code. For example, mathematical simplification and a search through all possible cases are different routes.

sections.heading: LLM-assisted classification.
sections.text: We use a two-stage process to identify each response’s strategy and group responses that follow the same route. Before classification, we remove generated follow-up user/assistant turns and replace mathematical answer statements and values, or GPQA choice labels, with placeholders. In Stage A , GPT-5.6-Luna with high reasoning effort reads each response separately, describes its primary strategy, and selects supporting parts of its reasoning or code. These descriptions form the input to Stage B , where the same model groups base and RL responses by strategy within each question and assigns a shared route label to each group. Stage B uses the descriptions rather than the original responses, with model identity, correctness, and explicit final-answer labels hidden. Both stages use fixed prompts for each subject area and a new Codex CLI session ( codex exec ) for each labeling call. For quality control, GPT-5.6-Sol with high reasoning effort independently checks whether the Stage A descriptions are supported by the response text and whether Stage B has incorrectly combined or separated routes. Descriptions and labels that fail these checks are corrected and checked again. Shortened prompt templates appear in Section E.3 .

sections.heading: Route counts with equal sample sizes.
sections.text: For Figure 3 (a), we compare the number of distinct routes using equal numbers of identifiable responses from both models. For each question, we set the common sample size to the smaller number of identifiable responses available from the two models. We average the number of distinct routes over all subsets of that size for each model, then average equally over questions within each benchmark and across the full set. When both models have 16 identifiable responses, this simply counts the distinct routes among all 16 responses. The overall mean weights benchmarks by their question counts.

sections.heading: Routes not found in base samples.
sections.text: For Figure 3 (b), we compute the fraction of each question’s 16 RL responses whose primary route does not appear in its original 16 base responses, then average over questions. The overall fraction is 487 of 3,840 RL responses (12.7%).

sections.heading: Confidence intervals.
sections.text: We use 5,000 bootstrap resamples of questions for each benchmark and the full set. Questions are sampled with replacement, keeping their base and RL measurements together. The 95% confidence intervals use the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap estimates for each panel’s means and the paired mean difference reported in Section 3.1 . Route labels stay unchanged during resampling.

sections.heading: E.2 Examples of route changes after RL
sections.text: These are the two examples discussed in Section 3.1 . Both have 16 identifiable responses per model, so the route counts use all responses without sample-size adjustment.

sections.heading: Concentration on a route found in base samples.
sections.text: In livecodebench-0088 , the task is to minimize | nums ⁡ [ i ] − nums ⁡ [ j ] | \displaystyle|\mathrm{nums}[i]-\mathrm{nums}[j]| subject to | i − j | ≥ x \displaystyle|i-j|\geq x . Eight base responses binary-search a sorted list and compare neighboring values, six compare index pairs with nested loops, and two use indices sorted by value. All 16 RL responses use the binary-search route, reducing the observed route count from three to one.

sections.heading: Use of a route not found in the base sample.
sections.text: In livecodebench-0163 , the task is to find positions where pattern a \displaystyle a appears within distance k \displaystyle k of a position where pattern b \displaystyle b appears. All 16 base responses compare pairs of matching positions directly. Five RL responses use the same method, while 11 use binary search over the list of positions where b \displaystyle b appears to find the lower end of [ i − k , i + k ] \displaystyle[i-k,i+k] . This gives one observed route for base and two for RL; the 11 binary-search responses are counted as using a route not found in the base sample.

sections.heading: E.3 Shortened prompt templates
sections.text: These templates summarize the instructions for both stages and describe the output fields in plain language. Stage A: describe one response’s strategy (shortened) Input. The question, one cleaned response, and its response ID. 1. Read the entire response on its own. Describe only methods it carries out or specifically proposes; do not solve the question or judge correctness. 2. Choose the method used for the final conclusion or submitted program. If unclear, choose the most developed method, then the first method supported by reasoning or code. 3. Describe the initial approach, problem representation, and main solution step, without final-answer values or quality judgments. 4. Copy supporting reasoning or code exactly and link each claim to its supporting text. Mark the response as “no route” if no method is attempted, or “unclear” if the method cannot be identified. Output (main fields). Return a JSON list with one record containing the response ID, route status (one route, a route change, no route, or unclear), how the primary route was selected, starting approach, problem representation, main solution step, short strategy summary, and supporting text linked to each claim. Stage B: group responses into routes (shortened) Input. The question and its ID, plus the Stage A strategy descriptions for all base and RL responses to that question. 1. Use these descriptions to group responses by their primary strategy. Do not infer model identity or correctness. 2. Group responses under the same route when they differ only in notation, calculation errors, completeness, wording, or whether the same method is carried out by hand or in code. Separate routes only when the initial approach, problem representation, or main solution step differs. 3. Assign every response ID to exactly one group. Choose group members before naming routes, and describe the strategy shared by every member. 4. Place responses marked “no route” or “unclear” in a separate group for responses without an identifiable route. Output. Return a JSON record containing the question ID and a list of route groups. For each group, give its name, a one-sentence strategy description, and the IDs of its responses. Copy every response ID exactly.

sections.heading: Appendix F Empirical Analysis of Theoretical Predictions
sections.text: This appendix examines empirical evidence for the transfer, coverage, and scaling predictions of Sections 4 , 5 and 6 , respectively.

sections.heading: F.1 Transfer and forgetting across tasks and models
sections.text: We examine the task- and model-dependent transfer and forgetting predicted by Section 4 , using cases that illustrate differences in target-task requirements and teacher–student compatibility.

sections.heading: Protocol violations in tool use.
sections.text: ToolUse requires a specified Action name and structured Action Input arguments [ shenfeld2026selfdistillation ] . One prompt requests five facts about the physical characteristics of axolotls, together with source URLs. Qwen3-14B-Base produces one Action: getAxolotlFacts call, with arguments specifying the category “physical characteristics” and a limit of five, and is graded correct. Qwen3-Math-RL first produces the same call, then adds “Please provide the output from the getAxolotlFacts tool,” simulates further interaction, and repeats calls. These additional calls cause the response to be graded incorrect. The change from issuing a single requested call to simulating further interaction turns a correct initial action into an unsuccessful response. This example helps explain the ToolUse decline in Table 1 : additional generated interaction can reduce performance on a task requiring a precise tool call, even as mathematical performance improves.

sections.heading: Errors in factual verification.
sections.text: HaluEval requires a “Yes” or “No” judgment on whether a candidate answer contains hallucinated information [ li2023halueval ] . One item includes the question “Which magazine was started first Arthur’s Magazine or First for Women?” The accompanying background information identifies Arthur’s Magazine as a periodical published in 1844–1846. The candidate answer is “First for Women was started first,” whereas the dataset’s reference answer is “Arthur’s Magazine.” Qwen3-14B-Base correctly responds “Yes”, while Qwen3-Math-RL incorrectly responds “No”. Both outputs satisfy the required label format; the error is the acceptance of a false chronological comparison. This gives a concrete example of the HaluEval decline in Table 1 : gains in mathematical problem solving can coexist with poorer judgment of a supplied answer’s factual accuracy, reflecting the different requirements of the target task.

sections.heading: Compatibility between teacher and student models.
sections.text: Qwen3-14B-Base and Gemma-3-12B-IT are trained with SFT on the same 40K mathematics demonstrations obtained by rejection sampling from Qwen3-32B. Gemma-3-SFT declines on all 14 OOD benchmarks, whereas Qwen3-SFT declines on ten and improves on four ( Table 1 ). Gemma’s losses are also substantially larger on several benchmarks. The difference therefore concerns both the breadth and severity of forgetting across tasks. In Eq. 4.9 , the teacher policy determines the demonstrated strategies, while the student’s feature overlaps determine their support on a target prompt. Identical demonstrations can therefore lead to different sets 𝒮 E ​ ( x ′ ) \displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{E}(x^{\prime}) for the two students. Theorem 4.3 relates forgetting to whether these sets retain strategies valid for the target, and Eq. A.22 shows that the probabilities within each set also depend on the student’s initial strategy preferences on training and target prompts. The shared Qwen model family offers a plausible explanation for better compatibility with the Qwen student: the teacher’s demonstrated strategies may be closer to its initial preferences. Imitating these demonstrations can then preserve strategies useful beyond mathematics for Qwen while reducing their probability in Gemma, explaining the selective transfer of Qwen3-SFT and the broader, more severe forgetting of Gemma-3-SFT.

sections.heading: F.2 Prompt-level Pass@ N \displaystyle N analysis
sections.text: We examine the finite-budget coverage predictions of Section 5 , focusing on how gains and losses on questions with rare successes change benchmark coverage. For the benchmark distribution ℬ \displaystyle\mathcal{B} , any policy π \displaystyle\pi satisfies the exact identity Pass ​ @ ⁡ N ⁡ ( π ) − Pass ​ @ ⁡ N ⁡ ( π 0 ) = 𝔼 x ′ ∼ ℬ ​ [ ( 1 − R π 0 ​ ( x ′ ) ) N − ( 1 − R π ​ ( x ′ ) ) N ] . \operatorname{Pass@}N(\pi)-\operatorname{Pass@}N(\pi_{0})=\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{B}}\left[(1-R_{\pi_{0}}(x^{\prime}))^{N}-(1-R_{\pi}(x^{\prime}))^{N}\right]. (F.1) Thus the aggregate reversals in Figure 2 reflect changes in the distribution of per-question success probabilities. We examine per-question records to show how gains and losses on individual questions produce these benchmark-level reversals.

sections.heading: Training-data dependence: CodeContests.
sections.text: On CodeContests, the Qwen base model and Math RL model produce at least one correct response for 238 \displaystyle 238 and 240 \displaystyle 240 of the 377 \displaystyle 377 questions, respectively; Math-Code RL does so for 228 \displaystyle 228 questions. The base model solves 22 \displaystyle 22 questions for which Math-Code RL produces no correct response, while Math-Code RL solves 12 \displaystyle 12 questions for which the base produces no correct response. The following examples illustrate the two outcomes: • Loss of coverage. codecontests-1192 requires summing pairwise absolute differences for up to 10 5 \displaystyle 10^{5} inputs. The base answers it correctly in 375 \displaystyle 375 of 1,024 \displaystyle 1{,}024 samples. One correct program generated by the base model sorts the inputs and computes the sum in O ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ n ) \displaystyle O(n\log n) time. None of the 1,024 \displaystyle 1{,}024 Math-Code RL responses is correct; every generated program times out. • Gain of coverage. codecontests-1332 requires finding the minimum number of subset toggles needed to turn on the lamps in each prefix of an array. Math-Code RL answers it correctly in 74 \displaystyle 74 of 1,024 \displaystyle 1{,}024 samples, whereas none of the base responses is correct. Theorem 4.1 provides an interpretation of these outcomes in terms of strategy selection. For codecontests-1192 , a correct base response uses a sorting strategy z sort ∈ ℳ ⁡ ( x ′ ) \displaystyle z_{\rm sort}\in\mathcal{M}(x^{\prime}) . By Eq. 4.5 , training changes its odds relative to competing strategies, with each training prompt’s contribution weighted by its feature overlap with the target. Training on code problems can therefore reduce the probability of selecting this efficient algorithm if these weighted updates favor competing strategies. For codecontests-1332 , the same mechanism can increase the probability of selecting a strategy that solves the lamp problem. Eq. 4.6 expresses both effects in the vanishing-KL limit by conditioning the base policy on 𝒮 ⁡ ( x ′ ) \displaystyle\mathcal{S}(x^{\prime}) : this can increase or decrease the probability assigned to valid strategies in ℳ ⁡ ( x ′ ) \displaystyle\mathcal{M}(x^{\prime}) . Pass@1 nevertheless increases from 19.7 % \displaystyle 19.7\% to 31.6 % \displaystyle 31.6\% ( Table 2 ). With only 12 \displaystyle 12 newly solved questions among 377 \displaystyle 377 , most of this increase must come from higher average accuracy on the questions solved by both models.

sections.heading: Base-model dependence: AIME 2025 and BoxNet.
sections.text: Under Math RL, sampled AIME 2025 coverage rises from 23 / 30 \displaystyle 23/30 to 25 / 30 \displaystyle 25/30 for Qwen but falls from 20 / 30 \displaystyle 20/30 to 18 / 30 \displaystyle 18/30 for Gemma. In the vanishing-KL limit of the transfer model, RL conditions the base policy on strategies favored by training ( Eq. 4.6 ). The probability of selecting a valid strategy rises or falls according to whether valid strategies have a larger or smaller share of probability within this set than in the original policy. Different initial strategy preferences and feature overlaps can therefore produce opposite changes under the same training mixture. BoxNet also differs across base models ( Table 2 ): Qwen improves Pass@1 from 3.8 % \displaystyle 3.8\% to 9.9 % \displaystyle 9.9\% and observed Pass@1024 coverage from 34 / 100 \displaystyle 34/100 to 51 / 100 \displaystyle 51/100 , while Gemma lowers Pass@1 from 9.1 % \displaystyle 9.1\% to 7.3 % \displaystyle 7.3\% but expands coverage from 16 / 100 \displaystyle 16/100 to 30 / 100 \displaystyle 30/100 . For Gemma, the 16 questions solved by both policies lose 2,819 \displaystyle 2{,}819 correct responses, exceeding the 1,011 \displaystyle 1{,}011 gained on 14 newly solved questions. Thus successes become spread across more questions but less frequent overall, explaining the opposing changes in the two metrics ( Eq. F.1 ). In boxnet-0098 , the prompt requires moving red, blue, and green boxes to their targets, with the blue box first moved to an adjacent square [ stojanovski2026reasoning ] . The base has 0 / 1024 \displaystyle 0/1024 successful responses, whereas Gemma RL has 749 / 1024 \displaystyle 749/1024 . In one matched pair, the base plan delivers only the red box, while the RL plan completes all three deliveries, including the blue box’s intermediate move. Both outputs are valid fenced JSON. This example makes the target’s requirements concrete: a useful planning strategy must account for the prerequisite move and all three goals ( Theorem 4.1 ). Together, these records show different question-level outcomes behind the aggregate curves. The same Qwen Math RL model loses observed coverage on two AIME 2024 questions but gains it on two AIME 2025 questions. Math-Code RL increases accuracy on some CodeContests questions and decreases it on others. Gemma’s Math RL model broadens coverage on BoxNet while lowering accuracy on questions solved by both models. These records illustrate changes in coverage across tasks and models, with differences in runtime outcomes, plan completeness, and the distribution of correct responses across questions.

Yixiao Huang 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Hanlin Zhu Somayeh Sojoudi Affiliation: University of California, Berkeley Affiliation: {ziheng_cheng,yixiaoh,hanlinzhu,sojoudi}@berkeley.edu Abstract Recent studies on reinforcement learning (RL) report seemingly conflicting evidence about large language model (LLM) reasoning. Training on mathematics can improve performance in other domains, yet gains in Pass@1 can coincide with lower Pass@ N \displaystyle N than the base model. This raises a fundamental question: does RL expand an LLM’s reasoning boundary, or merely reweight its existing reasoning space? We revisit these phenomena across Qwen and Gemma model families, showing both cross-domain gains and forgetting, while coverage at large sampling budgets increases on some tasks and decreases on others. Detailed analysis of solution traces before and after RL indicates a shift in the reasoning strategies the model employs, motivating a two-stage autoregressive policy model that separates strategy selection from problem-specific execution. Within this framework, we prove how RL’s implicit bias reshapes strategy preferences, allowing gains on some tasks while suppressing strategies required by others. This mechanism can also broaden or narrow coverage at a given sampling budget even without expanding strategy support. We further provide theoretical justifications for log-sigmoid and log-linear scaling laws in RL compute, and evaluate their predictive power. Together, these results connect changes in strategy selection to cross-domain transfer, reasoning coverage, and compute scaling. 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) has improved the performance of large language models (LLMs) on reasoning tasks ( shao2024deepseekmath ; deepseekai2025r1 ; yu2025dapo ) . RL updates a model using reward feedback on sampled responses, rather than training it to imitate demonstrations. Its success on mathematics and coding raises a broader question about how RL reshapes LLM reasoning. What accounts for these gains remains debated. RL may teach a model new ways to reason, or make it more likely to use reasoning it can already produce. For example, RL training on mathematical problems can improve performance in other domains ( huan2025transferability ) , but such gains are compatible with either interpretation. Sampling provides another perspective. Gains in one-shot accuracy (Pass@1) can accompany lower Pass@ N \displaystyle N , the fraction of problems solved within N \displaystyle N sampled attempts ( yue2504does ) , while prolonged training has been reported to broaden coverage ( liu2025prorl ) . These findings motivate the central question. Does RL expand an LLM’s reasoning boundary, or merely reweight its existing reasoning space? Our experiments show that training can improve performance in its own domain while reducing performance on other tasks or lowering Pass@1024 ( Figures 1 and 2 ). Comparing Qwen trajectories before and after RL indicates a shift in the model’s preferences among reasoning strategies ( Section 3.1 ). This motivates a two-stage policy model that separates strategy selection from problem-specific execution. Within this framework, we characterize how the implicit bias of RL reshapes strategy preferences, improving performance on some tasks while suppressing strategies required by others. We also contrast this mechanism with supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Our focus on how strategy preferences generalize across tasks complements the analyses of training-prompt sharpening and coverage ( chen2026reshaping ; chen2025coverage ) . Crucially, this reweighting mechanism explains coverage shifts without introducing new strategies. Pass@ N \displaystyle N at large N \displaystyle N is especially sensitive to problems with low success probabilities. Amplifying or suppressing rare valid strategies can broaden or narrow benchmark coverage, even as Pass@1 improves. Recent studies also examine how performance scales with RL compute ( khatri2025scalerl ; meta2026musespark ) . Our framework connects strategy selection to scaling laws, showing that selection dynamics admit log-sigmoid and log-linear approximations. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We document task-specific RL transfer and forgetting alongside divergent coverage shifts, with outcomes dictated by the training data, evaluation benchmark, and base model ( Section 2 ). • We analyze Qwen solution trajectories and find changes in which strategies are sampled for a question, motivating a separation of strategy selection from execution ( Sections 3.1 and 3.2 ). • Theoretically, we characterize RL’s implicit bias in strategy selection and derive conditions for transfer, forgetting, and expansion or shrinkage of coverage at a given sampling budget ( Sections 4 and 5 ). • We derive local approximation bounds for log-sigmoid and log-linear scaling laws and evaluate how well the fitted curves predict performance later in training, showing that predictive reliability varies with the training mixture and evaluation domain ( Section 6 ). 2 Empirical Evidence on Transfer and Reasoning Coverage The extent to which RL transfers beyond its training domain and expands the reasoning boundary remains actively debated. In this section, we revisit these phenomena across various model families and task domains to show that these seemingly contradictory findings can be reconciled. 2.1 Experimental setup Models and datasets. Our experiments use Qwen3-14B-Base ( yang2025qwen3 ) and Gemma-3-12B-IT ( gemmateam2025gemma3 ) as base models. We train both models on 48K mathematics problems from UniReason ( huan2025transferability ) (Math RL). For Qwen, we also train a variant on this dataset augmented with 5K curated coding problems from Eurus-2-RL ( cui2025process ) (Math-Code RL). For comparison, we also train both models with SFT using 40K mathematics demonstrations obtained by rejection sampling on Qwen3-32B responses ( huan2025transferability ) . Training setup. For all RL experiments, we train with GRPO ( shao2024deepseekmath ) using verl ( sheng2024hybridflow ) for 200 steps at a learning rate of 10 − 6 \displaystyle 10^{-6} . Each step samples 512 prompts and generates 16 responses per prompt (up to 16,384 tokens), followed by one epoch of actor updates with a minibatch size of 128. For SFT, we train for 1.5 epochs using a batch size of 512 and a learning rate of 5 × 10 − 5 \displaystyle 5	imes 10^{-5} . Further training details are given in Appendix D . Evaluation protocol. We evaluate transfer using benchmarks of mathematics, coding, knowledge and planning, and general capabilities. Our default inference settings use temperature 0.6, top- p \displaystyle p 0.95, and a maximum generation length of 32,768 tokens, though specific benchmarks retain their original protocols such as greedy decoding. Section D.2 gives the benchmark list and complete task-specific sampling and scoring details. 2.2 Cross-domain transfer and forgetting Figure 1 : Transfer and forgetting depend on the benchmark, training data, and base model. Each column reports changes in performance from the base model after training. RL consistently improves in-domain performance, but transfer behavior beyond the mathematics and coding domains varies significantly. In contrast, SFT exhibits catastrophic forgetting across a broad range of domains. Figure 1 illustrates the transfer and forgetting results. While RL consistently improves in-domain math performance, out-of-domain (OOD) behavior diverges significantly. Incorporating coding data into training (Qwen3-Math-Code-RL) improves coding tasks but fails to yield universal transfer. Moreover, despite identical training data, Qwen3-Math-RL and Gemma-3-Math-RL shift in opposite directions on many OOD tasks. SFT results exhibit similar model dependence: Qwen3-SFT shows selective transfer on knowledge and planning despite broad forgetting elsewhere, whereas Gemma-3-SFT suffers universal OOD degradation. Together, these results indicate that training-domain success does not reliably predict OOD outcomes. Instead, transferability emerges from the complex interaction among training data, evaluation benchmark, and base model . Complete scores are reported in Table 1 . Although prior work suggests that RL can generalize better to OOD tasks than SFT ( huan2025transferability ; chu2025sft ) , our findings highlight that RL remains susceptible to forgetting, with the direction and magnitude of OOD performance changes varying substantially across settings ( chen2026retaining ; shenfeld2026razor ) . 2.3 Expansion and shrinkage of finite-budget coverage Figure 2 : RL can either expand or contract reasoning coverage at large sampling budgets. Higher Pass@1 can accompany either lower or higher Pass@1024 relative to the base model. The direction of the coverage change varies across training mixtures, benchmarks, and base models. Task-level gains and losses show how training changes performance across domains. To examine how it changes the range of problems solved within each task, we compare coverage at different sampling budgets using Pass@ N \displaystyle N ( Figure 2 ). For a fixed prompt, Pass@ N \displaystyle N increases with Pass@1; however, benchmark-level comparisons do not necessarily preserve the Pass@1 ordering at large N \displaystyle N . Reduced coverage at large sampling budgets. The most prevalent pattern we observe is higher Pass@1 alongside lower Pass@1024 relative to the base model, especially in mathematics. This agrees with the coverage contrast reported by yue2504does . Broader coverage when base success is rare. On the Reasoning Gym task BoxNet ( stojanovski2026reasoning ) , where the base model’s success is exceptionally rare, Qwen3-Math-RL raises Pass@1 from 3.8% to 9.9% and Pass@1024 from 34.0% to 51.0%. Gemma-3-Math-RL also raises Pass@1024 coverage, although its Pass@1 falls. Qwen’s joint gains show that higher one-shot accuracy can accompany higher Pass@1024, consistent with liu2025prorl ; wen2026reinforcement . Our observations are broadly consistent with prior work ( liu2025prorl ) : shifts in Pass@ N \displaystyle N are largely dictated by the benchmark distribution and the base model’s initial ability, with substantial gains generally emerging where initial coverage is low. We further find that the training data itself can alter this regime: Qwen3-Math-RL and Qwen3-Math-Code-RL move CodeContests coverage in opposite directions. Consequently, whether RL expands or shrinks finite-budget coverage is context-dependent, rather than a universal RL effect or a trend that can be inferred from Pass@1. We examine the solution trajectories underlying these contrasts in Section 3.1 . 3 From Empirical Observations to Reasoning Strategy Selection To understand the performance and coverage changes in Sections 2.2 and 2.3 , we compare solution trajectories before and after RL. The comparison indicates a shift in the strategies used to solve a question. We describe these strategies as reasoning routes and examine how their use differs between the base and RL models. The findings motivate a model that separates strategy selection from conditional answer generation ( Section 3.2 ). 3.1 Reasoning-route analysis 3.1.1 Analysis setup We compare Qwen3-14B-Base with Qwen3-Math-RL on 240 questions from six benchmarks, with 16 responses per model and question. A reasoning route is the strategy used to reach a response’s final conclusion, when identifiable. Route identity reflects the problem representation and key mechanism, not notation, arithmetic, or final answers. For example, analytic reduction and exhaustive search are different routes. For each question, we combine both models’ strategy descriptions extracted by an LLM from their reasoning traces and group them by route. We average the number of distinct routes over equally sized samples of identifiable responses from both models, using the smaller number of identifiable responses available for each question, and then average equally over questions. Separately, we check which RL routes appear among the question’s original 16 base responses. Appendix E gives classification and statistical details. 3.1.2 Empirical findings Figure 3 : RL uses fewer routes, but also routes absent from base samples. (a) Mean numbers of distinct routes, using equal numbers of identifiable responses from both models for each question. (b) Percentage of RL responses whose route is absent from the same question’s 16 base responses. RL concentrates on fewer routes per question. Figure 3 (a) shows lower mean route counts for Qwen3-Math-RL on all six benchmarks, with the largest decreases on coding benchmarks. Across questions, the mean falls from 3.24 for the base model to 2.66 for RL, with a paired difference (RL minus base) of − 0.58 \displaystyle-0.58 (95% confidence interval [ − 0.78 , − 0.38 ] \displaystyle[-0.78,-0.38] ). For example, a LiveCodeBench question asks for the minimum absolute difference between array elements at least x \displaystyle x indices apart. Its 16 base responses use three routes, including comparison of neighboring values found by binary search, which all 16 RL responses use. RL also uses routes absent from the base samples. Of 3,840 Qwen3-Math-RL responses, 487 (12.7%) follow a route absent from the base responses to the same question ( Figure 3 (b)). CoT prompting and self-consistency establish the value of generating and sampling reasoning trajectories ( wei2022chain ; wang2023selfconsistency ) . Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains models using automatically checked task outcomes; Tülu 3 incorporates this approach into an open post-training recipe ( lambert2024tulu ) . shao2024deepseekmath introduces GRPO, and DeepSeek-R1 demonstrates large-scale reasoning gains from RL ( deepseekai2025r1 ) . DAPO and Open-Reasoner-Zero further develop open systems for scaling RL training on reasoning tasks ( yu2025dapo ; hu2025openreasonerzero ) . liu2025understanding examine how base-model capabilities and biases in GRPO affect training, and introduce Dr. GRPO to improve token efficiency. Transferability, forgetting, and the reasoning boundary. chu2025sft find that RL trained with outcome rewards generalizes better than SFT to unseen textual rules and visual variants in arithmetic and navigation tasks. huan2025transferability find that RL transfers more broadly and retains performance better than SFT in controlled experiments, while cheng2025crossdomain show that transfer varies with training domain and task difficulty. chen2026retaining identify on-policy data as a major factor in RL’s relative resistance to forgetting. Coverage findings also differ: yue2504does observe gains at small sampling budgets but reduced coverage at large ones, whereas liu2025prorl report expansion under prolonged RL training. wen2026reinforcement further show that evaluating reasoning correctness, rather than final answers alone, can change coverage comparisons. Our framework characterizes conditions for these contrasting outcomes within a shared model of strategy selection, distinguishing coverage at a given sampling budget from the creation or loss of underlying strategies. Scaling laws in reinforcement learning. khatri2025scalerl fit log-sigmoid curves relating compute to performance and validate extrapolation to longer RL runs. Meta’s Muse Spark reports log-linear gains in training scores with increasing RL steps ( meta2026musespark ) . tan2026scaling study joint scaling with model size, data, and compute in mathematical reasoning, while shen2026understanding relate the returns from increasing RL compute to pretraining. These studies establish empirical scaling relationships, but do not derive the commonly used log-sigmoid and log-linear forms from RL training dynamics. Our work provides a theoretical justification for both forms by deriving them as approximations to the dynamics of reasoning strategy selection, with explicit error bounds. We also examine their predictive reliability across evaluation domains. Theoretical analyses of RL in LLMs. chen2026reshaping analyze the selection of reasoning patterns in a two-stage tabular policy with fixed conditional success rates, focusing on behavior on training prompts. Complementary analyses study how gradient gaps affect optimization stability ( suk2025optimization ) , success amplification under GRPO ( mroueh2025grpo ) , and pretrained response coverage ( chen2025coverage ) . Our framework learns both strategy and answer policies and uses shared prompt features to derive how source updates reweight target strategies. This mechanism connects strategy selection to transfer and forgetting, Pass@ N \displaystyle N coverage, and scaling laws that describe performance over a limited range of training compute. 8 Conclusion and Discussion In this paper, we investigate how RL reshapes LLM reasoning. Starting from empirical observations across model families and task domains, we analyze solution traces before and after RL, showing a shift in the distribution over reasoning strategies. We propose a two-stage policy model to formalize this phenomenon and prove the conditions under which RL can transfer or forget capabilities and expand or contract finite-budget coverage. We also use this model to give a theoretical justification for empirical scaling laws in RL compute. These results connect changes in strategy selection to cross-domain transfer, reasoning coverage, and compute scaling.
